zones.label: Column 1

Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent scan reading; the returned transcription and notes are reviewer-authored, not a reproduction of the index.

runs.text: lhas fazem o ninho na borda do telhado. i, Dẽ-

lines.note: Continues f286's Aquellas abe- and its lhas catchword: the insects make their nests at the roof's edge. The scan supports telhado and a period before explanatory i; Dẽ- begins dentro on the next row.

runs.text: tro dos aguieiros de banbus onde dizem que

lines.note: Completes dentro and describes cavities in bamboo. The middle letters of aguieiros are abraded, so the aligned reading is retained with caution; printed banbus is not normalized to bambus.

runs.text: metem hum bichinho, & o matão, & depois

lines.note: The account says that the insects place a small creature inside, kill it, and then act upon it. This is the dictionary's reported explanation, not an endorsement of its account of insect development.

runs.text: ofomentão de maneiralque nace hũa abelha da

lines.note: Continues the reported belief that tending the small creature produces another bee. The scan has a tall, partly broken l-like mark between maneira and que; maneiralque is retained as an apparent printed anomaly, not repaired to the expected phrase. The close-set ofomentão is also preserved.

Completes the claim that the resulting insect is of the same kind as this jigabachi. The name is visibly italic here inside Portuguese prose; its initial is read as capital I by comparison with the nearby italic Iiga reference.
This separate jiga entry means oneself or I myself, unlike the insect name of the preceding entry. The initial is capital I, not lowercase l.
The insect name refers back to Iiga. Both Vide and the cited name are italic in the scan; Iiga is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese cross-reference.
Jigai is defined as killing oneself, explicitly ware to mi wo korosu. The headword begins Iigai, not OCR higai; the Portuguese phrase continues into the next row.
Completes aſsi meſmo and gives jigai suru as the verbal example. Vt is italic, while the Japanese example is upright.
Jigan means compassionate eyes, explained by jihi no manako. Enlargement shows initial capital I followed by dotted i in Iifino; the historical fi spelling matches the charity entries on f286.
Completes miſericor-dioſos, merciful or compassionate. The short row belongs to the Iigan definition.
This jijo entry means two women, explicitly futari no onna. It is distinct from the homograph below meaning a girl.
The example says that two women contend over one man. Ichinan is the single man, and araſô is the historical verb form for contending.

runs.text: andão apos hum homem contendendo entreſi.

lines.note: Completes the translation: the two women pursue one man while contending with each other. Entreſi is kept close-set as in the source, without modernizing spacing or adding accents to apos.
This homograph is a young girl, explained by chigio, onago, and a young female. The printed Voſonai is retained rather than being regularized to an expected modern osanai.
The one-word Portuguese gloss confirms that the preceding entry means a girl. Minina is historical spelling, not an error to replace with menina.
Jigō denotes one's own deeds. The example jigō jimet expresses bringing about one's own destruction through those deeds; Des- begins its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: truirſe por ſeus proprios feitos, ou obras aßi

lines.note: Completes Des-truirſe and says that a person's own acts bring about self-destruction. The beta-like double-s sort in aßi is preserved rather than replaced by two inferred long-s types.
Completes aßi meſmo, referring destruction back to the agent. This short row is part of the example under the first Iigô.
A separate jigō entry is glossed more generally as deeds or actions, with shiwaza as its Japanese equivalent. It is not merged with the previous headword despite identical spelling.
The expression means from now on or henceforth. The source's single-word pordiante is retained instead of modern por diante.
Jigai here means outside the temple, explicitly tera no hoka. It is distinct from Iigai, the earlier entry on self-killing; the printed guai spelling is preserved.
Adds varela, the dictionary's word for a Buddhist temple, as an alternative to monastery. This completes the location definition rather than introducing a new term.
Jige means resolving or understanding something oneself, explicitly mizukara toku. The headword begins Iigue, not OCR Figue; the Portuguese describes solving a doubt independently.
Completes the definition and gives jige jitoku su, understanding and attaining something oneself. The closing S. is upright and marks written usage; it is not part of the italic gloss.

runs.text: Aparição como de Anjos, ou foto-

lines.note: Jigen here means an apparition or manifestation, illustrated by angels or a hotoke. The Japanese religious term fotoque is printed in italics within the Portuguese explanation and is divided after foto-.
Completes foto-que from the preceding row. Que is therefore part of an embedded Japanese term, not the Portuguese conjunction in this instance; the italic type is retained.
This homograph means one's own words, explicitly mizukara ga kotoba. The scan supports double zz in Mizzucaraga; pa- begins the Portuguese noun on the next row.
Completes pa-lauras, words. The historical u spelling is retained, and this continuation is not promoted to an entry.
Jigetsu is the second lunar month, equated with nigatsu. The headword ends in checked-coda t plus punctuation, not the OCR's extra i; Ii- begins its example below.
Completes jigetsu no yuki koromo ni mitsu, with the second month's snow filling or covering the garment. The Portuguese begins a less literal explanation of abundant snow.

runs.text: do Niguachi he muita em abundancia. S.

lines.note: Completes the translation as abundant snow in Niguachi, the second month. Niguachi is italic within Portuguese prose; the closing upright S. marks written usage.
Jigi means ceremonial courtesies or politeness. Policia here concerns civilized manners, not the modern police; the Japanese example begins after the pilcrow.
Completes jigi wo totonoyuru, arranging or performing courtesies. Cor- begins corteſias, another Portuguese expression for courteous behavior.

runs.text: teſias. ¶ Item, Preparar, ou fazer a-

lines.note: Completes cor-teſias, then adds preparation as another sense of the same expression. A- begins aparelho on the next physical row.
Completes a-parelho and speaks of preparations for the courtesies or hospitality. Agaſolha continues without a visible terminal hyphen; none is supplied solely because the word continues.
Completes agaſolha-dos, then introduces jigihō, the rules of polite conduct. The last Iigui begins the example continued below; it is not embedded in the Portuguese gloss.

Completes the phrase about a person who does not know the rules of etiquette. Enlargement favors a worn caron in fǒuo, correcting the OCR circumflex; the faint left branch of the mark remains a minor uncertainty.
Completes the translation as not knowing the rules of courtesy. This makes the manners-related sense of policia explicit.

runs.text: Iiguiǒ. l, jiſo. Iino catachi. F

lines.note: Jigyō and the alternative jiso concern the shape of a written character, explicitly ji no katachi. Enlargement supports final o without a secure vowel mark. The subsequently consulted NINJAL index likewise records unaccented jiso and notes an intended jisǒ; the printed anomaly is not normalized.
Completes fei-ção da letra, a character's shape. The example jigyō ga yoi says that the form of the writing is good.
Completes the Portuguese explanation of good letter-shapes. The two near-synonyms feição and forma are retained rather than condensed.

This homograph concerns one's own acts or practice, explicitly doing something oneself. The initial of voconǒ has the pointed v-form in the scan; the historic spelling is not normalized to modern okonau.
Adds exercises and penitential practice to the preceding sense of personal deeds. The Portuguese wording indicates that religious practice is among the intended applications.
Jiin denotes a temple and associated hermitages or individual houses. The headword has capital I followed by i and a printed hyphen; ermidas does not contain the OCR's extra n.

runs.text: lares de Bonzos que estão ao redor na meſma

lines.note: Completes particu-lares and describes dwellings of Buddhist clergy surrounding the temple within the same enclosure. Bonzos is the dictionary's historical Portuguese terminology.
Completes the description with the shared enclosure. The short body line is distinct from the unrelated next-column homograph Ii-in.

This jiin is glossed as one's own sexual emission, corresponding to self-stimulation rather than the temple buildings of the previous entry. The printed hyphen and double-l spelling pollução are retained.
Jizen means in front of the temple, explicitly tera no mae. The initial capital I has been restored from the OCR's lowercase l.
Completes the alternative Portuguese designation as monastery. The inherited st spelling is retained for the dedicated typography review rather than globally changed to long s.
Jiji means at each time or hour. The example starts jiji kokkoku; coc- continues as cocuni on the next physical row.
Completes jiji kokkoku ni henzuru, changing at every moment. The literal Portuguese gloss begins as changing each hour.
Adds very frequently as the idiomatic interpretation of the preceding example. This clarifies that the phrase need not denote a measured sixty-minute interval.
Jijin is explained as mercy, love, and compassion. The three Portuguese nouns are distinct printed equivalents and are not condensed.
Jijitsu denotes time and day, with toki and hi as the Japanese equivalents. The final t is retained as a checked-coda spelling; the example is physically divided after Iijit-.
Completes the instruction to do this without letting time pass. The Portuguese translates the command in terms of uninterrupted action; isto retains its aligned st form.
Completes the instruction as acting without interruption and without ceasing. Interpolação has the contextual sense of an intervening break, not textual interpolation.
Jijū is described only as a particular dignity or rank. The caron over u is visible; no duties or institutional details absent from the gloss are added to the transcription.
Jiju means receiving something oneself, explicitly mizukara ukuru. The Portuguese ends in pormĩ, with the abbreviation mark over i rather than the OCR's u; S. is an upright written-usage label.
Jijuyō combines receiving and using for oneself. The printed synonym is mizukara uke mochiyu, and the Portuguese begins with using something.

runs.text: ſeruirſe da couſa que hum fez. Bup

lines.note: Completes the explanation as making use of something one has made. Bup. is upright and identifies Buddhist terminology; the label is not part of the italic sentence.
Jiman is self-conceit, explicitly being proud of oneself. The Portuguese has abbreviation tildes in Preſũção, including the mark over u missing from the OCR.

runs.text: vãa gloria. ¶ Item, Louuor proprio. Vt,

lines.note: Adds vainglory and self-praise as senses of jiman. The historic double-a form vãa is kept, and the pilcrow introduces the additional definition before its example.
Jiman kikinikushi says that self-praise is unpleasant to hear. The Portuguese likewise says that praising oneself sounds bad, with the reflexive phrase continued below.
Completes the reflexive phrase referring self-praise back to the speaker. The single long-s form aſi is retained, without harmonizing it with the nearby aßi spelling.
Jimen denotes the surface or face of writing, explicitly ji no omote. The gloss starts with the visible appearance of a character or written text.
Completes the reference to writing and adds literal meaning as another sense. The pilcrow separates that semantic extension from the preceding physical description.
Jimetsu means self-destruction, with onozukara messuru as the explanation. The aligned mixed long-s/short-s spelling meſsuru and Portuguese Distruirſe are retained rather than regularized.
Completes the reflexive definition and supplies jimetsu suru. The whole word Vide is italic; Iigô is an upright cross-reference to the earlier entry on one's own deeds.
Jimon means asking oneself. The scan visibly separates Mizzucara and tô, which the OCR had joined; the latter bears a circumflex.
Jimon jitō suru means posing and answering one's own question. The Portuguese begins with putting the doubt to oneself, then continues to resolving it.

runs.text: porſi ſoltala, como quẽ estuda ſoo, & argu-

lines.note: Continues with resolving the doubt oneself, as someone studying alone and reasoning privately. The scan has a separate ſoo with two o letters, not the joined OCR estudaſo; the aligned st spelling in estuda is retained.
Completes argu-menta conſigo, reasoning or debating with oneself. The historical reflexive construction explains the self-questioning example rather than introducing another activity.

This jimon means a temple gate, glossed by tera and kado. Enlargement confirms that the second Tera is italic inside the Portuguese explanation; only that occurrence is an embedded typeface-review term.

runs.text: Botar hum meſmo o vinho que ha de be

lines.note: Jimori means pouring for oneself the wine one is going to drink. The physical row ends be without a visible hyphen; the remainder ber follows below.
Completes be-ber and gives jishaku, jimori as the Japanese example. The abbreviated hũ begins the Portuguese description of a person serving himself.

runs.text: ſi o copo, & ovinho, & fazer por ſi officio

lines.note: Continues with taking the cup and wine oneself and performing the attendant's work. The opening has a visible separation ſi o; ovinho remains close-set, and the scan supplies the missing initial o of officio.
Completes the description as doing the cupbearer's work. Enlargement shows the single-storey italic a in eſcanção, rather than the OCR's o; the neighboring final o supplies a shape comparison.
Jimotsu denotes the temple's belongings or furnishings, explicitly tera no mono. Alfayas is used for such equipment or possessions, not narrowly for modern jewelry.
This jin means a human being or person, matched by hito and homem. The scan shows initial I, not the OCR's F; it remains distinct from the moral-virtue entry that follows.

runs.text: Hum dos cinco primores, ou bõs custumes,

lines.note: This jin is the moral quality of benevolence or humaneness. The dictionary introduces it as one of five excellences or good practices; bõs preserves its abbreviation mark.

runs.text: & virtudes moraes dos Iapoẽs, & Chinas que

lines.note: Continues by describing these as moral virtues of the Japanese and Chinese. Iapoẽs retains the printed nasal abbreviation, and Chinas is the source's historical designation.

runs.text: conſiste em ajudar ao proximo compadecendo

lines.note: The definition begins with helping one's neighbor and feeling compassion. Compadecendo continues with its reflexive pronoun on the next row, without an added hyphen.

runs.text: ſe delle, & amandoo, mas eſquecendo ſe de ſi

lines.note: Completes compadecendo-ſe and adds loving the other person while forgetting oneself. Amandoo retains the printed attached pronoun, rather than modern amando-o.
Completes the definition as forgetting oneself and one's own concerns. Miz- starts the Japanese example; its remaining letters continue on the next physical row.
Completes mizzukara wo wasure and continues with loving others and those in danger. The object ayauqiuo receives its verb ſucui on the next row.
Continues with rescuing those in danger and helping those in distress or extremity. Subete mono begins the general statement about all things or circumstances below.

runs.text: ni naſaqeuo ſaqito xi, cotoni furete aua-

lines.note: Says to put compassion first in all things and on each occasion. Aua- begins awaremi, compassion or pity, whose remainder follows on the next line.

Completes awaremi no kokoro and concludes that possessing such a compassionate heart is called jin. The caron in yǔ is retained, and this row closes the long Japanese explanation rather than starting another entry.
This jin refers to the kidneys, also jin no zō. The whole Portuguese word Rins is italic; the OCR's internal roman segment does not represent a Japanese insertion.
Jinai means inside the temple, explicitly tera no uchi. The definition parallels other temple-location entries without merging their separate headwords.
Completes the alternative Portuguese description as inside the monastery. The inherited long-s spelling is retained for later specialist typography review.
Jinan means the second son. The short Portuguese gloss is complete on this physical row.
Jinba means a person and a horse, with hito and uma supplied separately. The signature and Iinba- catchword below are page furniture, not a further body line belonging to this entry.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: Iinba- is the isolated bottom-right catchword. Its role is established from placement and typography; the following page is outside this package and has not been independently inspected.
